New machine. Its objects are: mosogo, femada, luriser, gipevos, bezuzu, fakakan.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects at once, to see how the machine responds to a group.

TEST: mosogo, femada, luriser
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group lit up. Next I'll test the other three objects, which will help narrow down the rule. For example, it will show whether one nexiom is enough or whether both are needed together.

TEST: gipevos, bezuzu, fakakan
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Both halves lit up separately, so the rule cannot require both nexioms together. Most likely one nexiom is in each group, and a single nexiom is enough to light the machine. Now I'll narrow down the first group by testing one object alone.

TEST: mosogo
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Mosogo lit up by itself, so a single nexiom is enough to light the machine. That makes mosogo very likely a nexiom. If so, the other nexiom should be in the second group: gipevos, bezuzu or fakakan. I'll test those one at a time.

TEST: gipevos
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Gipevos didn't light up alone, so it is not a nexiom. Assuming any single nexiom lights the machine, the second nexiom is either bezuzu or fakakan. Testing bezuzu alone will settle it: if it lights up, bezuzu is the nexiom, and if not, fakakan is.

TEST: bezuzu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Bezuzu lit up by itself. Gipevos alone did not light the machine, and objects that are not nexioms never affect it, so a group with no nexiom does not light up. That means any object that lights the machine alone must be a nexiom. Mosogo and bezuzu both did this, and there are exactly two nexioms, so I don't need the last test.

ANSWER: nexioms = mosogo, bezuzu
One last question. If only bezuzu were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Yes. I already tested bezuzu by itself, and the machine lit up. The machine responds to its nexioms in a fixed way, so the same test should give the same result.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: dobedun, segokal, bamubas, fopili, kunenik, vomabu.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll begin by testing a single object on its own to see how the machine reacts.

TEST: dobedun
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

Dobedun alone didn't light it, but I don't yet know the rule (whether one nexiom is enough or both are needed). Next I'll test half the objects together to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: segokal, bamubas, fopili
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The trio segokal, bamubas, fopili lit up, so at least one nexiom is among them (and if the machine needs both nexioms, both are there). Testing one of the three alone will help tell whether a single nexiom is enough to light the machine.

TEST: segokal
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Segokal alone lit the machine, so segokal is a nexiom and a single nexiom is enough to light it. Dobedun alone didn't light, so it is not a nexiom. That leaves bamubas, fopili, kunenik and vomabu as candidates for the second nexiom. Testing bamubas and fopili together will show which pair it is in, and one more test will then settle it.

TEST: bamubas, fopili
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Bamubas and fopili together lit the machine, so the second nexiom is one of those two. Kunenik and vomabu are ruled out. This also rules out a rule where the machine lights only for exactly one nexiom: under that rule, the earlier trio with segokal would have held both nexioms and stayed dark. Testing bamubas alone will settle which of the two it is.

TEST: bamubas
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Segokal alone lit, and so did bamubas alone. If one nexiom is enough to light the machine, then segokal and bamubas are the two nexioms, which fits every result so far.

There is one other rule that also fits: the machine lights only when no nexioms are present. Under that rule every object that lit is a non-nexiom. Dobedun, which stayed dark, would be a nexiom, together with either kunenik or vomabu.

To tell these apart, I'll test dobedun and segokal together. If one nexiom is enough, segokal makes it light. If the machine lights only with no nexioms, dobedun keeps it dark.

TEST: dobedun, segokal
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Dobedun and segokal together lit up. That rules out the "lights only with no nexioms" rule, because dobedun would have been a nexiom on the machine and it should have stayed dark.

The rule that fits all six results is that the machine lights when at least one nexiom is present:
- Dobedun alone stayed dark, so dobedun is not a nexiom.
- Segokal alone lit, so segokal is a nexiom.
- Bamubas alone lit, so bamubas is a nexiom.
- The other tests that lit (segokal, bamubas and fopili; bamubas and fopili; dobedun and segokal) each contained segokal or bamubas, so they also fit.

Two other rules are ruled out:
- "Lights only for exactly one nexiom" would have kept the segokal, bamubas, fopili test dark.
- "Lights unless exactly one nexiom is present" fails too. Dobedun alone staying dark would make dobedun a nexiom. Dobedun and segokal lighting would then make segokal the second one. But then segokal alone would hold exactly one nexiom and should have stayed dark, and it lit.

ANSWER: nexioms = segokal, bamubas
One last question. If only bamubas were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Yes. I already ran this exact test (bamubas alone), and the machine lit up. That fits the rule I found: bamubas is a nexiom, and one nexiom is enough to light the machine.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: sozivon, pegabo, kovezol, gumipar, lemulen, dimasen.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half the objects to see whether the machine responds to that group.

TEST: sozivon, pegabo, kovezol
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The first three didn't light it up. Next I'll test the other three objects together to compare.

TEST: gumipar, lemulen, dimasen
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Both nexioms are probably among gumipar, lemulen and dimasen. I'm assuming the machine reacts when at least one nexiom (or both) is present. The first group not lighting fits that, but under an unusual rule the nexioms could still be in the first group. I'll now test single objects to work out which ones matter and how the machine responds.

TEST: gumipar
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Gumipar lights the machine on its own, so it is almost certainly a nexiom. This also rules out two possible rules: "both nexioms must be present" and "exactly one nexiom lights it." If the machine lights whenever at least one nexiom is present, the first result means the second nexiom must be lemulen or dimasen. I'll test lemulen alone to find out which.

TEST: lemulen
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Gumipar lights the machine on its own, and lemulen alone does not. If the machine lights whenever at least one nexiom is present, lemulen is not a nexiom, so the second one should be dimasen. One other rule also fits all four results: the machine responds to only one particular nexiom (gumipar). In that case the second nexiom could be any object. Testing dimasen alone checks this directly. If it lights, dimasen is confirmed as a nexiom.

TEST: dimasen
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Gumipar and dimasen each light the machine on their own. Lemulen does not, and neither does the group of sozivon, pegabo and kovezol. All five results fit the rule that the machine lights whenever at least one nexiom is present. Since exactly two objects are nexioms, they must be gumipar and dimasen. I don't need the last test.

ANSWER: nexioms = gumipar, dimasen
One last question. If only dimasen were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Yes. This was observed directly, not inferred. My fifth test put dimasen alone on the machine, and it lit up. Assuming the machine behaves the same way each time, it would light up again.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: ribikal, rokuges, guguru, finusa, lapenak, sotabur.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll begin by testing half of the objects together to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: ribikal, rokuges, guguru
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The set {ribikal, rokuges, guguru} lit up, so at least one nexiom is among those three. I don't know the rule yet: the machine might light for any single nexiom, or only when both are present. Testing one object alone should help separate these possibilities.

TEST: ribikal
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first test lit up, so at least one nexiom is among ribikal, rokuges and guguru. Ribikal alone did not light. That means either ribikal is not a nexiom, or the machine needs both nexioms present at once.

Testing rokuges alone is the next useful check:
- **If it lights:** rokuges is a nexiom, and a single nexiom is enough to trigger the machine.
- **If it doesn't light:** either guguru is the nexiom, or the machine needs both nexioms present at once.

TEST: rokuges
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Here is where things stand:
- **Test 1:** ribikal, rokuges and guguru together lit up, so at least one nexiom is in that group.
- **Tests 2 and 3:** ribikal alone and rokuges alone did not light.

That leaves two kinds of explanation:
1. **One nexiom is enough to light the machine.** Then neither ribikal nor rokuges is a nexiom. Guguru must be one, and the other is finusa, lapenak or sotabur.
2. **The machine needs both nexioms present.** Then both nexioms are among ribikal, rokuges and guguru.

Testing guguru alone separates these. If it lights, I can test the remaining three objects one at a time with my last two tests. If it doesn't, two pair tests will settle it.

TEST: guguru
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Guguru alone lit up, so **guguru is a nexiom**, and a single nexiom seems to be enough to light the machine. If that rule holds, ribikal and rokuges are not nexioms, since they failed alone. The second nexiom is then finusa, lapenak or sotabur.

With two tests left, I'll check them one at a time:
- If finusa lights, it is the other nexiom.
- If not, I'll test lapenak. If lapenak doesn't light either, sotabur is the nexiom.

TEST: finusa
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Finusa lit up alone, so it is the second nexiom. Guguru and finusa are both nexioms:
- **Ribikal alone did not light.** A test with no nexioms present does not light the machine, because non-nexioms never affect it.
- **Guguru and finusa each lit up alone.** So each must be a nexiom, since an object without nexiom status would behave like an empty test.

Exactly two objects are nexioms, so I don't need the last test.

ANSWER: nexioms = guguru, finusa
One last question. If only finusa were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Yes. I already ran this exact test: finusa alone lit up. The machine responds to its nexioms in a fixed way, so placing finusa on it by itself again should give the same result.

PROBE: yes
